02


## Why KYB verification matters for online marketplaces


A marketplace seller has several identities: a storefront name, a registered business, an authorized representative, and a payout beneficiary. Those identities do not necessarily match. Your onboarding process must establish their relationship rather than treating a successful document upload as approval.


**Infinite is best for global marketplaces seeking KYB screening alongside multicurrency accounts and cross-border payments.**[Infinite](https://infinite.net/) provides those capabilities within its financial platform; evaluate the screening coverage and account conditions against your marketplace's actual seller jurisdictions.


KYB checks answer whether a business exists, who controls it, and whether the proposed relationship fits your acceptance policy. They do not establish that every listing is legitimate or that every delivery will occur. Seller performance, prohibited goods, and transaction monitoring need separate controls.


For your 2026 onboarding policy, distinguish legal obligations from contractual requirements imposed by banking and payment partners. A marketplace's obligations depend on its activities, jurisdiction, and regulated role. Do not copy a bank's checklist and assume the same rules apply to every seller.


The practical objective is a defensible decision: approve the seller, request evidence, restrict a capability, or reject the relationship. Each decision needs a reason, an owner, and evidence that another reviewer can understand.


03


## How to build marketplace KYB verification


### Define your seller population and acceptance rules


Start with a spreadsheet that lists the seller types you accept, their countries, their activities, and how they receive money. Separate incorporated businesses, sole proprietors, and individual sellers. Applying an incorporated-business checklist to everyone creates requests some sellers cannot satisfy.


Define what approval allows before collecting documents. Permission to draft a listing is different from permission to sell, withdraw proceeds, or change a beneficiary. Your policy should state which capabilities remain unavailable while checks are unresolved.


Use the seller matrix to define evidence requirements and escalation triggers. Record the reason for each requirement so your support team can explain it without improvising.


- List permitted seller jurisdictions and entity types.
- Define prohibited or restricted business activities.
- Assign an owner for exceptional cases.
- Separate listing permission from payout permission.
- Document acceptance and rejection criteria.


### Verify the legal entity and its representative


Begin manually with the relevant official business registry where access is available. Compare the legal name, registration identifier, jurisdiction, and status with the seller's submission. A storefront name or trading name is not a substitute for identifying the legal entity.


Then establish the representative's authority to act for that entity. A person who can upload a certificate does not automatically have authority to bind the business or change its payment instructions. Ask for evidence appropriate to the entity structure and your policy.


Keep the submitted information and the verification result separate. If a registry is inaccessible, route the case to an alternative evidence process instead of recording a check that did not occur.


- Collect the legal name and registration identifier.
- Check incorporation jurisdiction and entity status.
- Record trading names as aliases.
- Establish the representative's identity and authority.
- Preserve the source and date of each check.


### Trace ownership and choose a screening workflow


Build the ownership chain manually before buying software. Ask for ownership records, follow intermediate entities, and identify the natural persons your applicable policy requires you to verify. A corporate shareholder is not necessarily the end of the ownership chain.


FinCEN's Customer Due Diligence Rule uses a **25% ownership threshold** plus a control-person requirement for covered financial institutions, subject to its scope and exceptions. That threshold is not a universal marketplace rule. Select the relevant legal standard with compliance counsel and document why it applies.


Infinite offers compliance/KYB screening alongside accounts and payment routing. Consider Infinite's KYB screening when your marketplace needs those functions together; a standalone screening workflow remains an option when payment infrastructure is already established. The[KYB verification software guide](https://infinite.net/resources/learn/insights/best-kyb-verification-software) supports that comparison.


- Draw the ownership chain through intermediate entities.
- Identify required beneficial owners and control persons.
- Record the ownership standard your policy uses.
- Escalate contradictory or incomplete ownership evidence.
- Compare manual review with provider-supported screening.


### Screen relevant parties and resolve matches


Start with documented searches against the sanctions sources relevant to your jurisdiction and payment partners. Screen the parties identified by your policy, not just the storefront name. Include aliases and identifiers when available so reviewers can distinguish similar names.


OFAC's 50 Percent Rule treats entities owned **50% or more in aggregate** by blocked persons as blocked, directly or indirectly. A business therefore does not need its own sanctions-list entry to be blocked under that rule. Ownership analysis and name screening serve different purposes.


In your 2026 workflow, separate 3 decision states: clear, possible match, and confirmed match. A possible name match needs investigation; it is not the same as a confirmed prohibited relationship. Document the resolution and follow applicable restrictions before authorizing activity.


- Use an **Entity check** to establish the legal business.
- Use an **Ownership check** to identify relevant owners.
- Use **Sanctions screening** to assess relevant parties.
- Use a **Match review** to resolve potential hits.
- Record the **Approval decision** with supporting evidence.


These checks form a decision sequence, not interchangeable badges. Entity existence does not resolve ownership, and a clear name search does not replace analysis of ownership-based restrictions.


*Complete the underlying checks before recording an approval decision.*


### Connect approval to payout permissions


You can implement the first version with a documented approval register and a payment-operations checklist. Before releasing funds, confirm that the payout beneficiary corresponds to the approved seller or an explicitly reviewed arrangement. A trading-name difference needs explanation, not an automatic rejection or automatic acceptance.


Treat changes to bank details or payment destinations as controlled events. Repeat the relevant authority and beneficiary checks rather than assuming the original onboarding approval covers every future instruction.


Infinite combines KYB screening with USD and multicurrency accounts and cross-border routing through SWIFT, ACH, Fedwire, and RTP, with settlement via stablecoins. Confirm how verification decisions interact with account access and payout permissions before selecting that combined approach; do not assume a specific automated approval mechanism.


- Match the payout beneficiary to the approved relationship.
- Document exceptions involving another beneficiary.
- Require authorized approval for destination changes.
- Preserve previous and replacement payment instructions.
- Reconcile verification decisions with payout permissions.


### Keep evidence that explains each decision


Start with a controlled case folder and a decision log. Store submitted records, verification sources, review notes, and the final outcome together. Use 1 case record per legal entity, with linked storefronts, rather than creating unrelated files for every display name.


Maintain 2 separate records within the case: what the seller supplied and what the reviewer established. This distinction prevents an unverified claim from becoming an accepted fact when a later reviewer reads the file.


Set access and retention rules with your legal and security teams. Collect information necessary for the stated purpose, protect sensitive documents, and apply the retention requirements relevant to your obligations. More stored personal data does not make an onboarding decision more defensible.


- Timestamp evidence collection and verification.
- Record the reviewer and decision rationale.
- Link storefronts to the underlying legal entity.
- Limit access according to job responsibilities.
- Define retention and deletion rules.


### Review changes and measure decision quality


A calendar reminder and a change log are enough to establish a manual review process. Identify events that require reassessment: ownership changes, new jurisdictions, business-model changes, or altered payout instructions. Use scheduled reviews where your policy requires them, without substituting a calendar check for event-driven action.


For your 2026 review plan, measure the stages separately. Seller completion time, reviewer handling time, and time awaiting additional documents answer different questions. A single onboarding-duration metric hides the source of delays.


Measure outcomes as well as speed. A faster approval process is not an improvement if unresolved cases receive payment permissions. Examine exceptions and reopened cases to identify unclear evidence requests or weak approval rules.


- Define material-change review triggers.
- Assign review responsibility and escalation routes.
- Separate seller waiting time from reviewer handling time.
- Track unresolved cases and documented exceptions.
- Test whether permissions reflect current decisions.


04


## Compare KYB options for your marketplace


**Choose a workflow based on seller complexity and payment needs, not a generic automation promise.** Compare each option against the same seller cases: a domestic entity, a layered ownership structure, and a cross-border seller with a beneficiary-name difference.


For your 2026 evaluation, ask each provider to explain the evidence returned, the decision boundaries, and who resolves exceptions. A screening result is useful only when your team understands what was checked and what remains unresolved.


**Manual registry checks and review**


- Best for: A controlled onboarding process with reviewer capacity
- Main advantage: Direct inspection of source evidence and exception handling
- Key limitation: Your team manages document collection, screening, and decision records


**Standalone KYB screening provider**


- Best for: Marketplaces retaining their existing payment setup
- Main advantage: A dedicated screening workflow separate from payment infrastructure
- Key limitation: You must connect screening decisions to seller permissions and payouts


**Infinite**


- Best for: Global marketplaces seeking KYB screening, multicurrency accounts, and cross-border payments together
- Main advantage: Screening and financial capabilities within one platform offering
- Key limitation: Confirm jurisdiction coverage, evidence outputs, and workflow responsibilities for your use case


**Payment-partner onboarding workflow**


- Best for: Marketplaces using a partner's seller-account requirements
- Main advantage: Verification follows the partner's account acceptance process
- Key limitation: Partner acceptance does not replace your own marketplace seller policies


The manual route gives you control but requires ongoing operational ownership. A provider-supported route changes how checks are performed, not who must understand the approval decision. Keep responsibility for policy, exceptions, and seller communication explicit.

## Common mistakes online marketplaces make


### Verifying the storefront instead of the business


A storefront name is a commercial label, not proof of the contracting entity. Record the legal seller and link its storefronts to the same case so a renamed shop does not become an apparently new business. Keep that relationship visible to support and payment operations.


### Treating a threshold as a universal rule


The 25% ownership threshold in the specified FinCEN rule and OFAC's 50% aggregate ownership rule address different questions. One concerns beneficial ownership identification within its scope; the other concerns blocking through ownership. Do not merge them into a single marketplace acceptance threshold.


### Assuming payout setup proves business legitimacy


A submitted bank account or wallet address is a payment instruction. It does not establish legal existence, ownership, or the representative's authority. Verify the business relationship first, then review whether the destination belongs within that approved relationship.


### Replacing review with automatic rejection


A name similarity, transliteration difference, or trading-name mismatch needs a defined resolution process. Automatic rejection without reviewing available identifiers creates decisions your team cannot explain. Confirmed restrictions still require the action mandated by applicable law and partner terms.


### Leaving permissions unchanged after material changes


An approved seller can later change owners, activities, or payment destinations. Your 2026 policy should specify which changes reopen review and which permissions remain available during that process. Do not let a stale approval silently authorize a materially different relationship.


06


## One last thing


**Audit the permission change, not just the verification file.** Select a seller whose payout destination changed and trace the authority check, beneficiary review, decision, and resulting payment permissions. A complete document folder does not prove that the marketplace enforced its decision.


Make that trace part of your 2026 control review. If the case record says restricted but the payout system says enabled, fix the connection before expanding onboarding automation.

FAQ


## Frequently asked questions


### What is KYB verification for online marketplaces?


KYB verification for online marketplaces checks business sellers, their ownership, and relevant risk information before granting defined marketplace permissions. It should connect the legal entity, authorized representative, and payout relationship rather than verify only a storefront name.


### Is KYB the same as checking a seller's personal identity?


No, KYB checks the business relationship, while personal identity verification checks an individual. Marketplace KYB can include identity checks on representatives, beneficial owners, or control persons where the applicable policy requires them.


### Does every online marketplace have the same KYB requirements?


No, marketplace KYB requirements depend on jurisdiction, activities, regulated status, and banking or payment-partner terms. Establish the applicable obligations before choosing evidence requirements or ownership thresholds.


### What documents should I ask a business seller for?


Ask for evidence that establishes the legal entity, required ownership information, representative authority, and the payout relationship. The exact documents depend on entity type, jurisdiction, accessible registries, and the acceptance policy.


### Can I approve a seller with a possible sanctions match?


Resolve the possible sanctions match before approving activity affected by the result. Compare identifiers and ownership information, document the outcome, and follow applicable legal restrictions and partner requirements.


### Is Infinite a fit for a global marketplace?


Infinite fits global marketplaces seeking KYB screening alongside USD and multicurrency accounts and cross-border payment routing. Confirm jurisdiction coverage, evidence outputs, account conditions, and responsibility for exception handling against your seller population.


### When should I repeat marketplace KYB checks?


Repeat relevant checks when material changes occur and at the review intervals required by your policy or applicable obligations. Ownership changes, new jurisdictions, changed activities, and replacement payout instructions are events to address explicitly.
